A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REFINESTAT research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated sections and renumbered tables.

before.justification: v1 reports original program-generation experiments, diagnostic and predictive results, component ablations, token-use measurements, and memorization-control experiments in Section 5.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds NumPyro run-rate and diagnostic evaluations in Section 5.5, Tables 5–6.

M1.justification: The specified semantic acceptance rule expands from three predicates in v1 Section 3.2 to six in v2 Section 3.1. Dependency, support, and type validity become additional rejection conditions, also reflected in Figure 1. This substantially expands the proposed filter; the two-phase refinement procedure and ELPD objective remain.

E1.justification: v2 Section 5.5 extends evaluated synthesis coverage from PyMC alone to NumPyro across all five benchmarks using Qwen-2.5-Coder–7B. This adds a second target programming environment with different library requirements. The underlying Eight Schools, Dugongs, Peregrine, Surgical, and GP datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Standard, SynCode, BoxLM, expert programs, OpenAI o3, and IterGen where previously evaluated. The added NumPyro experiments reuse Standard unconstrained generation; they introduce no new comparison method.

E3.justification: v1 Section 5.4 describes token costs for best-performing programs and cumulative ten-run batches, with separate REFINESTAT runs. v2 Appendix G.1 describes generating a program across five runs per method. This revises the reported selection and aggregation protocol without establishing reruns. Main diagnostic thresholds and baseline best-of-five selection remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix C adds a worked filtering/diagnostic example and a qualitative case study of three generated programs, examining added priors, nonlinear terms, and changed response variables. Existing component ablations, token analysis, memorization controls, and failure analyses are retained, often relocated.

E5.justification: Table 3 newly reports standard deviations for OpenAI o3. Its added REFINESTAT deviations were already available in v1 Table 2. The token study's repeated-run description also changes from ten-run batches to five runs per method; this does not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: v2 Tables 5–6 add a substantial set of NumPyro outcomes: at temperature 0.3, run rates are 0.35 for REFINESTAT versus 0.15 for Standard, and REFINESTAT produces valid GP programs where Standard fails. These extend results under a new backend. Retained PyMC values and the relocated token-efficiency and memorization tables are unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 formally defines dependency, support, and type predicates and extends their validity conjunction from three to six terms. Mathematical changes are localized to these conditions. The reliability score, valid-model space, ELPD objective, and diagnostic equations retain their substance; neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims: semantic constraints and diagnostic-guided refinement enable a single small open-weight model to synthesize reliable probabilistic programs and compete with larger-model baselines. The added evaluations do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of backend portability and structural exploration, including changing the observed variable. Section 5.4 also qualifies the memorization evidence as limited and the question as unresolved, although Appendix G.2 retains v1's stronger interpretation. Existing limitations concerning predictive checks and optimization guarantees largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 Section 9 newly reports source code in supplementary material and a planned open-source release. Section 3.2 also explicitly documents initial prior and likelihood generation through constrained decoding. Hardware, principal hyperparameters, and dataset-specific PyMC prompts are retained, with experimental settings moved to Appendix E.

R1.justification: v2 adds memorization and contamination references, including Dong, Golchin and Surdeanu, Li, and Kong. It also cites Mündler et al. (2025) and contrasts prefix/type validation with statistical reliability requiring full posterior inference. The established positioning against BoxLM and earlier probabilistic synthesis remains largely intact.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: extended background, experimental settings, failure discussion, token analysis, and detailed memorization results move into reorganized Appendices A–G. Numerous passages are condensed or rewritten, and v2 adds terminology explanations, worked examples, acknowledgments, and a reproducibility statement.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to display six validity checks. v2 adds two NumPyro tables, a semantic-filtering table, and boxed structural examples; expands Table 3 with uncertainty; and highlights selected Table 2 entries. Token and memorization tables move to the appendix, alongside substantial conference-format layout changes.

improvement.justification: The NumPyro experiments provide direct portability evidence, while o3 uncertainty reporting and clearer documentation improve assessability. The gains are limited by unchanged ablations for the expanded validation rule and revised token aggregation accompanying identical results. The new structural examples also change response variables without explaining comparable ELPD assessment, so their evidential benefit is less clear.
